title: Rate 1/5 Non-Malleable Codes against Entangled Split-State Tampering
abstract: We construct efficient information-theoretic non-malleable codes for classical messages that are secure against two noncommunicating local quantum tampering operations with arbitrary pre-shared entanglement. For every sufficiently small fixed $ξ>0$ and all sufficiently large first-share lengths $n$, the codes have rate at least $1/5-ξ$, perfect correctness, and error $2^{-n^{Ω(1)}}$. Security holds for every message, with a single message-independent simulator for each attack. This resolves the constant-rate question for worst-case classical messages in the entangled two-split-state model.   Our construction builds on the permutation-based two-split construction of Batra, Boddu, and Jain, which achieves rate approaching $1/5$ for uniformly random messages. We retain their architecture but replace the uniform message input to the permutation with a prescribed message concatenated with fresh uniform padding. Our main contribution is a worst-case security reduction for this modification.
summary: This paper develops a new construction for non-malleable quantum codes, proving they can securely encode classical messages at a rate approaching 1/5. It achieves this by modifying existing constructions to provide worst-case security guarantees against complex, entangled quantum tampering attacks. The methodology involves advanced quantum information theory tools to rigorously bound the information leakage during the attack.
main_problem: The paper addresses the construction of efficient information-theoretic non-malleable codes (NMCs) for classical messages that are secure against two noncommunicating local quantum tampering operations with arbitrary pre-shared entanglement.
main_result: The authors establish a worst-case security guarantee for such codes, achieving a rate of at least $1/5 - \xi$ for sufficiently large share lengths $n$. This resolves the constant-rate question for worst-case classical messages in the entangled two-split-state model.
method: The construction builds upon prior work using a permutation-based two-split structure, modifying it by concatenating the message with fresh uniform padding to achieve worst-case security. The security proof involves complex comparisons between actual and ideal quantum states using CPTP maps.
model_or_system: The model involves encoding a classical message into a quantum state structured in a 'two-split-state' form, which is then subjected to local quantum tampering operations. Security is quantified by bounding the trace distance between the actual and ideal states.
key_observables: Rate ($\geq 1/5 - \xi$), Error ($2^{-n\Omega(1)}$), and the trace distance ($\Delta(\mu, \sigma)$) quantifying security against tampering.
important_parameters: The rate $1/5$, the small positive constant $\xi$, and the large share length $n$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on techniques like the 'scalar mean-one lemma' in the quantum setting and the ability to replace maximum loss with an average deficit through padding randomness.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup involving two local quantum channels and the message-selection step, comparing state evolution ($ho_0 	o \mu Z \Lambda E_2$) and detailing the process of computing and normalizing the selected message state.
paper_structure: The paper develops the security proof by first analyzing the classical adversary using averaging over source-independent tapes, and then extending this to the quantum adversary by comparing actual and ideal quantum states using CPTP maps and smoothing techniques.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, high-rate bound for quantum information security primitives (NMCs) against sophisticated, entangled attacks, which is foundational for quantum cryptography and secure quantum communication protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The two local quantum channels have no communication link. Double lines carry classical registers; single lines carry quantum registers. The input on E1E2 is ψE1E2, independent of the encoding on X, (Y, C). Reserved classical copies are omitted; they are used only by the analyst. Dashed cuts label states. The smoothing in A2,ζ is a proof device, not part of the encoder.

Figure 2: Two equivalent preparations before tampering. The upper channel retains M, Z, X, Y, C and discards its padding register. The lower channel computes the same M from Z, C. Both preserve the indicated original classical values. Appending the same state ψE1E2 and applying the attack of Figure 1 preserves equality. There is no approximation or BBJ invocation in this figure.

Figure 3: Solid arrows apply the indicated CPTP maps. The bottom dashed connections are distance estimates, not physical operations that transform one state into the other. BBJ is applied at µ, before continuation and before any message selection. Only the original key is idealized; the entire side state on ΛE2 retains its actual marginal.

Figure 4: The top row computes the original message and selects M = m; the bottom row normalizes the selected state and computes the output symbol. The connector carries the same selected state from the top row to the bottom row; it performs no additional operation. CP-TNI means completely positive and trace-nonincreasing. Multiplication by q is an analytical normalization, not an outcome CP map on arbitrary inputs. The same maps act on the actual and ideal states.

Figure 5: The bottom estimate is the mean-one scaling factor theorem, not ordinary data processing of Tm. The two solid paths compose to the same CP map Φm. Only this map depends on the requested m; the states µ, σ, ν and the continuation were defined without it. All distances compare states on the same register space.
